query: The Poets' Supper {A society of village poets has taken the upstairs room for its yearly supper, and needs someone to judge the contest.|The poets are back. Their president remembers your verdict from last year and has not forgiven it.|The poets' supper again, and this year the contest is in rhyming couplets only, including the toasts.} The landlady says: whoever wins, the wine bill gets paid. Judge the contest {You give a prize to everyone, each for something different, and each of them thinks theirs is the real one. The wine bill gets paid with a flourish.|Your verdict, in rhyming couplets, gets a standing ovation. The president pays you himself and asks for a copy.|You find something true to say about every poem, even the long one about turnips. They tip in verse and in coin.} {You give the prize to the poem about the president's late wife. It was, it turns out, written by her rival. The supper ends early.|Your verdict starts an argument that becomes a fight that becomes a poem about you. It is not a kind poem.|Nobody agrees with you, loudly, in couplets.} Pour and listen {You pour wine and listen to forty poems. Three of them are good, and you remember one for weeks.|You keep the glasses full and the poets talking. You go home with fair pay and a head full of rhymes.|You pour and say nothing, and learn more about metre than a term of lectures taught you.}
